response:
I verified all three against the fixture source before ruling on them — the evidence strings check out exactly.

## The three findings

**1. `duplicated_navigation_source` — `crime_00006`, medium, conf 0.70 → BLOCK**

```
Evidence:
  · destination: /settings/billing
  · src/nav/registry.ts label: Plans
  · src/nav/sidebar.ts label: Billing
```

Confirmed: `src/nav/sidebar.ts:6` has `{ to: "/settings/billing", label: "Billing" }`, `src/nav/registry.ts:6` has `{ path: "/settings/billing", title: "Plans" }`. Two files, one destination, two different user-visible strings, no canonical owner.

This is the one that earns a block. It isn't a naming preference — it's two sources of truth for the same fact, which is exactly the failure mode `agent_risk` exists to catch. An agent told "rename Billing to Plans" greps for `label: "Billing"`, edits `sidebar.ts`, and leaves `registry.ts` untouched and now silently wrong. Deterministic detection, small unambiguous fix (`consolidate_nav_source`, risk: medium).

**2. `route_metadata_drift` — `crime_00007`, medium, conf 0.65 → WARN**

Seven evidence lines, all verified in `src/routes/settings/billing.tsx`: path `/settings/billing`, component `PricingPage`, `metadata = { title: "Plans" }`, `<title>Subscription</title>`, plus the two nav labels. Four competing names for one page.

Real, but the weakest case for a gate in the set — lowest confidence (0.65), nothing breaks at runtime, and "component name should match route name" is a defensible-to-disagree-with convention. Also, three of its seven evidence lines are the *same* nav disagreement as #1, so fixing #1 collapses most of this finding on its own. Warn, and ask the author to state the canonical term for the destination in the PR description.

**3. `docs_code_drift` — `crime_00033`, low, conf 0.90 → BLOCK**

```
· docs/teams.md:5 → ./setup.md (not found)
```

Confirmed absent — `docs/` contains only `billing.md`, `commands.md`, `teams.md`. Severity `low` understates this one: it's the highest-confidence finding of the three (0.90) because it's a binary fact, not a judgement, and the fix is either restore the file or delete the line. A broken link in the onboarding doc costs an agent a whole read cycle and teaches it that repo docs can't be trusted. Gate it — a check that can't false-positive and takes a minute to satisfy is the cheapest block you can buy.

## Nothing here is an ignore

None of the three is a false positive; I read the source for each. If you want the ignore-class item from this scan, it's the neighbouring cluster — `crime_00029/30/31` (`orphaned_destination` on `/account/subscription`, `/team`, `/workspace/members`, all conf 0.65). "Unreachable from nav, docs, or imports" is normal for in-flight pages, and the detector says so ("may be in flight"). Those are the ones to suppress with a reason, not these.

## Gate mechanics — one caveat

`--fail-on` thresholds on severity, not detector, so you **cannot** express "block #1, warn #2" — both are medium and fire together. In practice that's fine: same destination, same PR, one fix. If you want them genuinely separated:

```bash
crimes baseline save                                    # pin existing debt first
crimes baseline check --fail-on medium                  # blocks new #1 and #2
crimes ignore route_metadata_drift::src/routes/settings/billing.tsx \
  --reason "Component/page-title naming tracked separately; nav label drift is the gate"
```

And #3 at `low` will not fire under a `medium` gate — `--fail-on low` would catch it but also drags in the other 18 lows in this repo. Given all 37 findings here are pre-existing, the honest sequence is: baseline now, then gate new work at `medium`, and run the docs-link check as its own step rather than trying to get it out of `--fail-on`.
